abstract: Autism spectrum disorder is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition with strong genetic contributions and diverse social impairments. However, it remains unclear how autism-linked mutations alter social behavior across social contexts and relationships. Using SLEAP multi-animal pose tracking, we followed complete Shank3 knockout (exon 4-22 deletion) mice with adult male and female sibling cagemates over four weeks and with strangers. Unexpectedly, knockouts initiated more social contact and allogrooming with familiar cagemates. Individual differences in social behavior and preferences for specific cagemates remained stable over time across genotypes. With strangers, knockout mice showed less nose-to-nose contact, more nose-to-base contact, and more chasing. Unlike wild-type mice, knockouts did not increase contact with strangers relative to siblings. These genotype differences were not detected in conventional three-chamber sociability and social novelty assays. These findings reveal that Shank3 loss reshapes social behavior in context-specific ways, enhancing engagement with familiar partners while altering threat responses to social novelty.
